messages.subject: Stan ignoring prior information in starting chains? Or I don't know how to specify prior?
parts:
I have a big, complicated model, and when I tried to run it it failed to take a single successful step in over 1000 tries. I reduced the warmup to a very small number and found what I think is the problem: it was starting with values near 0 for some of the parameters that are quite far from 0...I'm still not sure why it couldn't move from there, but it should never have started there in the first place.  I trimmed away more and more of my model to try to find the simplest model that still has this problem and, well, here it is (see below): I have weak priors on the mean and variance of a few numbers, and I'm just trying to find the mean (mu) and standard deviation (sigma). It starts with a guess for mu that is close to 0, in spite of 0 being a long way away from the prior guess I've given it. This happens every time.

If I give this a large warmup then it works, but that's not a solution for me because it doesn't seem to be the case (with a warmup that takes several hours) for the problem that I really want to fit. 

Am I simply not understanding how to specify prior information? How do I get it to start a chain somewhere near where I think it should?

Instead of attaching separate files I've got it all right here (I call Stan from R):

ts_code <- '
data{
int<lower=0> nT; // number of data points
real y[nT]; //  data
}
parameters {
  real<lower=0> sigma; //
  real mu; // mean
}
model {
  sigma ~ lognormal(4,2); 
  mu ~ normal(20,5);
  for (t in 1:nT) { 
     y[t] ~ normal(mu,sigma);
  }  
}
'

parts:
On Wednesday, February 6, 2013 2:27:31 AM UTC-5, Phil Price wrote:
I have a big, complicated model, and when I tried to run it it failed to take a single successful step in over 1000 tries. I reduced the warmup to a very small number and found what I think is the problem: it was starting with values near 0 for some of the parameters that are quite far from 0...I'm still not sure why it couldn't move from there, but it should never have started there in the first place.  I trimmed away more and more of my model to try to find the simplest model that still has this problem and, well, here it is (see below): I have weak priors on the mean and variance of a few numbers, and I'm just trying to find the mean (mu) and standard deviation (sigma). It starts with a guess for mu that is close to 0, in spite of 0 being a long way away from the prior guess I've given it. This happens every time.
Yeah, there are a few examples on this list where this kind of thing happens.

If I give this a large warmup then it works, but that's not a solution for me because it doesn't seem to be the case (with a warmup that takes several hours) for the problem that I really want to fit. 

Am I simply not understanding how to specify prior information? How do I get it to start a chain somewhere near where I think it should?

You can always pass starting values explicitly via the init argument to stan(); otherwise they will be random on [-2,2] in the unbounded parameter space. Or you can center and / or rescale the data. But what I like to do in situations like this is to make the intercept a transformed parameter, as in:

ts_code <- '
data{
int<lower=0> nT; // number of data points
real y[nT]; //  data
}

transformed data {
           real y_mean;
           y_mean = mean(y);
   }
parameters {
  real<lower=0> sigma;
      real shift;
}
   transformed parameters {
      real mu;
      mu <- y_mean + shift;
   }
model {
  sigma ~ lognormal(4,2); 
  shift ~ normal(0,5); // note change to put prior on shift rather than mu
     y ~ normal(mu,sigma) // vectorizing this is much faster
}
'

Since shift is now the primitive parameter, starting it near zero will produce reasonable values of the log-posterior and the chain should be able to move around from there.

Ben

If I give this a large warmup then it works, but that's not a solution for me because it doesn't seem to be the case (with a warmup that takes several hours) for the problem that I really want to fit. 

Am I simply not understanding how to specify prior information? How do I get it to start a chain somewhere near where I think it should?

You can always pass starting values explicitly via the init argument to stan(); otherwise they will be random on [-2,2] in the unbounded parameter space. Or you can center and / or rescale the data.

Ben's mentioned the "unbounded parameter space." Under the hood, Stan is transforming the parameters written in your model to unconstrained variables. The transformations are described in detail in the manual in the chapter "Transformations of Variables" (page 220 of v1.1.1).

For example, the sigma parameter is defined to have a lower bound of 0. Section 32.2. "Lower Bounded Scalar" describes the transform: log(X-a), where X is the parameter and a is the bound. In your model, if no inits are supplied, log(sigma) will start somewhere random on [-2,2], which means sigma will start somewhere in the range [0.14, 7.4]. In warmup, Stan will tune its parameters based on the geometry of the log probability function. If a parameter like sigma starts far away from its mode, the magnitude of the gradient is going to be large and this is going to be problematic. This is where Ben's suggestion in using the transformed parameter comes in.

As Ben mentioned, another alternative is initialization. It is mentioned on Section 4.2 (page 22), but many of the BUGS examples have init files. One example is the rats model from vol1. If you've downloaded the Stan tarball, it is located at: src/models/bugs_examples/vol1/rats. It can also be found online at:
https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/tree/master/src/models/bugs_examples/vol1/rats

But what I like to do in situations like this is to make the intercept a transformed parameter, as in:
ts_code <- '
data{
int<lower=0> nT; // number of data points
real y[nT]; //  data
}
   transformed data {
           real y_mean;
           y_mean = mean(y);
   }
parameters {
  real<lower=0> sigma;
      real shift;
}
   transformed parameters {
      real mu;
      mu <- y_mean + shift;
   }
model {
  sigma ~ lognormal(4,2); 
  shift ~ normal(0,5); // note change to put prior on shift rather than mu
     y ~ normal(mu,sigma) // vectorizing this is much faster
}
'

Since shift is now the primitive parameter, starting it near zero will produce reasonable values of the log-posterior and the chain should be able to move around from there.

Surprisingly, I can't find this stated anywhere, if this is true. But at any rate it doesn't seem to be work. For the same simple mean, variance problem I described to start this thread, I created a file called stan.init.txt with my desired starting values:
mu <- 10.0
sigma <- 5.0

I then did
fit_test <- stan(model_code = ts_code, data=stan_test_dat,

iter=10,warmup=1,chains=1,init="stan.init.txt",verbose=TRUE)

The model compiles and runs but apparently does not make use of the initialization information: for the run I just tried, for example, its initial value for mu is -1.34.

I've also tried specifying initialization values using init=list(mu=10,sigma=5) but this generated an error, as I'm sure you would expect.

But I would certainly like to learn HOW to specify initial values, if you can tell me how to do that.

This seems like a pretty fundamental issue, to the extent that I'm surprised that I couldn't find examples in either the documentation or elsewhere in this forum. (I did find some recommendations to use init=0 or init="random" in a few places, but couldn't find any example of using init= to specify non-zero initial values). Has there been any thought of extending the Stan language to help with initialization? An obvious possibility, more easily said than implemented I'm sure, is that if a parameter is specified in the model block as having a distribution that is specified in terms of known distributional parameters, the starting value could be drawn from that distribution.  In the present instance, if I have

model {
  mu ~ normal(20,5)
  ...
} 

Then an initial value for mu could be drawn from a N(20,5) distribution. (Or, of course, mu ~ normal(mu_est,tau_est), where mu_est and tau_est are sent in as data would be a more common example in practice). This is what I assumed was happening, until you guys explained the initialization defaults to me. 

Or perhaps there's a good reason that's not done, or maybe it's number 8000 on the list of things to do in the future.

Anyway, I remain clueless as to how to specify initial values, in spite of having looked at the Rats example and forming an inits file that I thought was well-formed, and calling it in a way I thought would work. Not really sure what else to try (other than your patience, I mean).
